data.title: 2026/10/21(三)全台游資氾濫 為何會錢荒?股匯大矛盾!台幣越貶經濟越強？【早晨財經速解讀】
data.transcript_raw: Investors, welcome to Morning Financial  Interpretation. It is Wednesday,  October 21, 2026, 8:31 AM Taipei time.  Good morning everyone, I'm Hao. For  this half-hour session, we are here to  walk you through the shifts in global  financial news. The US stock market  shows mixed results; some positive  corporate earnings are emerging, and  oil prices are pulling back, though  they have stopped falling. There are  two angles we really need to watch. On  one hand, with earnings reports rolling  out, stocks aren't rising. Does this  mean P/E ratios are continuing to  decline? What level are we at now?  Secondly, let's look at Taiwan. The  depreciation of the New Taiwan Dollar  is a bit extreme this time, and selling  pressure from foreign investors is  quite heavy. How should we understand  an economy with 10%growth whose  currency is being sold off like this?  How do we interpret this major  contradiction in stocks and currency— the weaker the NTD, the stronger the  economy? On the other hand, we keep  talking about excess liquidity and how  ETF buying shouldn't be a concern, but  why is there a cash crunch? How can we  have both excess liquidity and a  shortage of cash at the same time?  Today, I'll share some observations  with our investor friends. Actually,  the US market seems to be attempting to  bottom out. Since big tech stocks— like those in the Nasdaq and S&P— haven't fallen yet, it represents a  degree of sector rotation from a market  cycle perspective, as big stocks  haven't softened yet. More importantly,  major stocks are now releasing their  earnings. If you observe closely, since  most stocks haven't hit new highs after  these reports, it results in a  continuous decline in P/E ratios. If we  look at the forward P/E ratio of the  Nasdaq for the next year, it has fallen  to 20.5 x. It was close to 25x at the  end of last year. What kind of level is  this 20.48 x? It’s already lower than  it was during the war earlier this year , roughly equivalent to the tariff war  levels of 2025, and has even returned  to the lows of the 2022 Russia-Ukraine  war. In other words, while it may not  be cheaper than the 2022 low, it is  roughly at its cheapest point in the  past four years. At this rate, once  this quarter's earnings are all  released, the P/E ratio could  potentially break through to 18 or 19  times. So, if we observe it from the  perspective of P/E valuation, it is  actually quite attractive. Of course,  some will factor in the high interest  rates in the bond market, arguing that  the higher the rates, the lower the P/E  should be, so a moderate mean reversion  is acceptable, as current benchmark  rates are indeed high relative to the  past 20 years. However, I think this is  a good reference indicator; at the very  least, it's not expensive, and you can  judge for yourself just how cheap it is . In fact, the Nasdaq 100 index has  returned to roughly the level it was at  around mid-September. The real pressure  point right now isn't actually about  liquidity risks or instability in these  large-cap tech stocks, but rather the  significant widening of credit spreads  in U.S. investment-grade bonds. If we  take a closer look at the CDS prices  for two major companies like Nvidia and  Broadcom, the speed of their increase  is incredibly fast. Looking at the 5- year credit default swap (CDS) spread,  it was about 35 to 40 basis points in  June, and by October it had......risen  to 98 to 144 basis points. The  insurance premium isn't exceptionally  expensive yet, but the point is that  the rate of increase is about three to  four times, hitting new highs for this  period in just six months. Broadcom's  credit hedging costs have increased by  about three times, yet the Nasdaq 100  index has only fallen by 5%, so why  hedge so much? This shows that a  certain group of people is clearly very  worried; they believe that since stock  prices haven't fallen yet, a catch-up  decline is highly likely, so they have  taken certain hedging measures in  advance. This is a direction we can  observe. If we look at the big picture,  regarding the overall North American  average investment-grade credit default  risk (CDX.IG), the spread has risen  from 50 basis points in September to  62.1 basis points now. This is a high —well, not an all-time high, as it  was higher during past financial crises , but it is a new high since March or  April of this year. So, while we don't  see a major impact overall, at the  individual stock level, there is a  sense that the credit market is  becoming more anxious than the stock  market. It seems quite a few people  believe that the index is not holding  up, and that it needs to catch up to  the downside; some people are saying  this, so we can monitor the situation  further. But conversely, if we think in  terms of P/E ratios, I’m actually  leaning more toward the buyer's side,  believing that buying at this rate of P /E decline won't lead to losses;  that’s my take. Right, looking at the  major U.S. stock indices, they are  actually still in a state of  consolidation. The Dow rose 529 points,  or 1.02%, to 52,495 points, slowly  pushing upward; the S&P rose 0.28%to  5,771 points, barely moving; the Nasdaq  fell 0.02%, closing essentially flat;  the SOX index fell 0.29%, closing at  11,283 points. It feels like it’s  trying to form a third base, holding  onto the platform area of this current  cycle. Now, everyone’s primary focus  is certainly on SpaceX’s revenue, as  the Q3 financial report shows revenue  of $ 14.58 billion, a 161% year-over-year increase. This is very  impressive. It is also higher than the  expected $ 12.72 billion. Net profit  reached $ 4.4 billion; compared to the  same period last year when it was still  posting a loss, it has now  significantly and substantially  improved. Earnings per share are around  45 cents, which is also far higher than  the market’s estimate of 13 cents.  Even more astonishing is that the  company projects next year's Q1 revenue  to reach $ 33 billion to $ 37 billion,  completely blowing past the market's  high expectation of $ 22 billion, which  is why the stock saw such a significant  boost after hours. The biggest  highlight of this financial report is  that SpaceX’s super intelligence  division saw Q3 revenue reach $ 7.5  billion, a growth of over 8 times  compared to the $ 800 million from the  same period last year, proving that AI  is actually very profitable. Although a  lot of money has been invested in AI,  the order volume from these cloud  enterprises placing orders with AI is  actually quite strong. As for leasing  AI data center computing power, its  main clients include a few, one being  Anthropic and the other being Google.  So, to some extent, even though there  is massive capital expenditure in AI,  it seems its clients are quite willing  to foot the bill. On the other hand,  satellite internet is, of course,  SpaceX's main source of profit; in Q3,  new subscribers increased by 13.6  million, internet business revenue hit  $ 5.25 billion, a 69%year-over-year  increase, and operating profit reached  $ 2.37 billion, far exceeding the  market's original estimate of $ 400  million, so I am quite satisfied with  this earnings report. Overall, the  stock price is now around $ 154,  slightly higher than the  volume-weighted average price since its  listing, but we must admit that since  the IPO, the stock has been under  significant pressure, and the standards  the market sets for SpaceX are  naturally...It needs to be higher than  the other seven giants, because its  core business revenue, compared to the  other six, is relatively not as strong  as imagined, or lacks the same momentum  in recurring revenue. In fact, before  the CS earnings report, there was  already a pessimistic tone in the  market, triggered by a Korean data  center IPO we saw yesterday, which was  valued at $ 750 million but crashed by  32%upon listing on Tuesday. People were  very worried; you have data centers,  government support, government  contracts, and profitable operations,  yet the market sold you off by 30%.  This series of market shocks created a  lot of pessimism, though the CS/SpaceX  earnings report managed to pull things  back slightly. But it’s very clear to  everyone now—while stock prices  haven't dropped much, the real focus is  actually on the credit market, where  hedging measures are being taken. So,  although there hasn't been much  volatility in stock prices, the market  seems fully prepared for potential  swings, which shows that the market is  clearly skeptical. Look at how after  Wave offered a 15%yield on its  five-year notes, the price of CDS ( Credit Default Swaps) climbed at an  astonishing speed. Now, the volume of  CDS contracts across the US has been  surging at a massive pace over the past  few months. Looking at the details— this is data from JPMorgan—take the  CDS trading volumes of heavyweights  like Google, SpaceX, Alphabet, Amazon,  Meta, Broadcom, and Nvidia. In July,  the weekly trading volume was around $  2 billion. By the end of September, it  hit $ 9 billion per week, a growth of  more than 3.5 times, and it continued  to hit highs in October. Why is  everyone suddenly rushing to buy  insurance against the potential default  of these giants? It's quite obvious.  Even if stock prices haven't surged  significantly, the cost of hedging is  rising. It’s not simply that because  stock prices went up, I'm buying more  insurance or more hedging. It actually  reflects growing market skepticism  about whether current cash flows can  sustain such massive capital  expenditures and debt burdens. This has  created an effect where, even if the  financial reports look great, it  doesn't prove that your risks are gone  or have disappeared. Because the point  is the money you've borrowed; the point  is not your current profit. I know the  profits are good, but I'm worried about  how much debt you've taken on. If  someone borrows money from you and says , lend me 1 million next year and I'll  pay back 1.15 million, don't you think  they might run off? CWF is just like  that. What if they offer a 20%yield? Or  25%? You’d feel something is off,  right? That’s why we say US CDS  trading volume is hitting new highs; it  stems from the market increasingly  doubting whether these small-to-medium  enterprises or AI startups can afford  such massive interest payments. Of  course, this pullback, especially for  the SOX index since the S&P didn't drop  much, does put some pressure on the SOX ; if you bought in the last quarter and  tell me you have zero positions, I  guess you probably missed out on this  year's market. So investing is the same ; you will always get a bit bruised  during market pullbacks. If you want to  know how pessimistic someone is about  the stock market, you don't need to  listen to what they say, just ask them  how much cash or what percentage of  their portfolio is in cash. If someone  is fully invested but keeps shouting  about a crash, it just means they're  worried; but conversely, if someone is  all cash and refuses to enter the  market, that is the true expression of  pessimism through action. For any  normal person this year, you must have  suffered some losses; anyone who didn't  get hurt this year is truly amazing. So  regardless, how much cash are you  holding? It often actually reflects how  much confidence you still have for the  future. If you go out with a girl, when  it ends, you might sneak a peek at her  phone's remaining battery; usually,  that’s the score she gives you. If  she’s willing to save the last bit of  battery for you, it means she’s  willing to keep talking, but if you  find there's almost no power left, it  means she’s long since stopped caring  about replying to you and is chatting  with other guys, and she doesn't care  about you anymore. So at this point,  you can understand that the amount of  cash you have on hand is, to some  extent, your level of pessimism toward  the stock market; this is something for  everyone to think about. Most people  will inevitably feel some pain  participating in this market, but it is  precisely because of that pain that you  are able to participate in this round  of the market. Despite the SOX dropping  so heavily, it remains the  best-performing index among major  indices this year. Alright, let's look  back at the Taiwan stock market. The  selling pressure is truly heavy, yet  it's impressive that it can still hold  its ground at this level. As of  yesterday, foreign investors had  cumulatively sold NT $ 2.03 trillion in  Taiwan stocks. This is the first time  it has broken the two-trillion mark.  That’s a massive milestone. In 2022,  they sold NT $ 1.2 trillion during a  full year of the Russia-Ukraine war and  high inflation, but this year, without  any major crises, they’ve sold two  trillion. Foreign investors have really  made it a habit to adjust their  positions in Taiwan stocks. They just  sell into any rally. In October alone,  they sold NT $ 662 billion. We see that  large-cap tech stocks are the primary  targets for liquidation; TSMC alone has  seen about NT $ 1.9 trillion pulled out  this year, so most of it is just  selling TSMC. Now, the key point is  that with foreign investors exiting so  rapidly, even though domestic ETF  buying is keeping up, it’s putting  immense pressure on the New Taiwan  Dollar exchange rate. We’ve seen the  NTD recently depreciate to around 32.6,  which is quite significant. We clearly  understand that foreign investors are  adjusting across the entire Asian  market, but it feels like the NTD is  undergoing a bit of catch-up  depreciation lately. Part of it, of  course, is that the Central Bank of  Taiwan hasn't raised interest rates.  While they haven't, the central banks  of Korea, Japan, Europe, and even the  US Federal Reserve have all raised  rates. Where does the money go? Water  flows downhill, and capital flows  toward higher interest rates. Therefore , the Central Bank of Taiwan really  hasn't had the power to keep capital  within the domestic banking system.  That’s the first perspective when  looking at foreign investors. And the  second perspective is that once we  observed the Taiwan stock market  performing relatively stronger than the  Korean market, it naturally became the  primary target for liquidation. If  you're going to adjust positions and  take profits on rallies, you naturally  pick the ones that have made money. For  foreign investors, the Korean stock  market hasn't exactly been profitable  this year, so whether it's the NTD or  the Korean Won, both are actually  sliding. Especially in the Korean  market, since the P/E ratio is already  low, foreign investors don't seem to  have much room for futures maneuvers  there. The NTD is different; the P/E  ratio for Taiwan stocks is actually  considered on the high side, so the NTD  might have more room for further  depreciation. Foreign investors feel  that the Taiwan market has a  particularly high appetite for buying  from retail investors, making it easy  to offload stocks. In contrast, for a  market like South Korea that is nearing  its bottom, foreign investors are  afraid to sell, fearing they might get  trapped themselves. Look at the KOSPI  index; it has fallen over 20%from its  peak and plunged 15%three times in a  year. Its price-to-earnings ratio  appears to have reached a historical  low. The P/E ratio for Taiwan stocks is  still over 20, but what is the 12-month  forward P/E ratio for the KOSPI index?  It’s 8.4 times, which should be the  cheapest point in history since 2008.  You might say, "But the KOSPI index  isn't right; stock prices are still  high, so how could it be at a 20-year  low?" The intuitive reason is that  their profits have surged. The decline  in the P/E ratio is driven both by the  fall in share prices and, more  significantly, by the rapid growth in  earnings. If we observe the details,  South Korean corporate profits are  still trending upward. Don't assume  that just because stock prices have  collapsed, corporate profits are  faltering; current earnings estimates  are still rising. Whether it's SK Hynix  or others, you can actually see a very  significant boost right now. As  mentioned earlier, whether you include  or exclude companies like Hynix and  Samsung, the average forward P/E ratio  is at its lowest point since 2008,  which gives investors something to  ponder. Of course, looking back at the  South Korean stock market, buying  interest is still a bit weaker compared  to the Taipei stock market. The reason  is simple; it's the same in investing:  once those who use leverage get hurt,  it takes a much longer time for them to  recover. Last time, people in the  Taipei stock market who wanted to  borrow money were forcibly reined in by  the Financial Supervisory Commission,  and they found it very difficult to get  loans. It’s the same with investing,  especially for those using margin  leverage. Sometimes we are certain that  a stock will rise, but we might be  forced to sell at the bottom due to  margin calls from falling maintenance  ratios. For those without leverage,  time is your friend. For those with too  much leverage, time becomes your enemy.  The scariest thing about investing is  not that the market won't recover, but  that by the time it does, you are no  longer in the market. That is why we  say you must stay alive. You must  survive; don't get the trend right only  to be wiped out by volatility. Isn't  there a famous saying about military  service? It goes: "Serving for twenty  months, dreading your girl sleeps with  someone else; others have all the fun,  I do all the work, who told me I don't  have any skills." It's just like  investing, where the worst part isn't  picking the wrong direction, but  picking the right one and waiting in  vain for the results! Knowing you're  about to be discharged, you can only  watch as the outside world keeps moving  and stock prices hit new highs, but you  no longer have the eligibility to stay  in the game—you've been washed out.  Right, so going back to what people are  more concerned about now: if the  devaluation of the NT dollar you  mentioned seems acceptable, and the  Korean stock market seems to have  specific individual stock issues— especially with retail investor frenzy —how do we explain why it's still so  hard to borrow money right now? What is  the actual state of Taiwan's  fundamentals? Actually, the latest  export orders have reached 114.2  billion USD, setting another historical  high, with a monthly increase of 0.9% and a year-on-year growth of 62%,  marking 20 consecutive months of growth . So, the influx of foreign exchange  from exports is still very fast. In  terms of surplus, there's a chance to  challenge 11 trillion NT dollars next  year, which is nearly triple the 3 to 4  trillion seen from 2023 to 2024; even  the surplus rate is rising. We estimate  that per capita GDP will challenge  50,000 USD next year; we were at 28,000  when the pandemic started, and now it's  50,000—that's an incredibly fast rise . So, looking at per capita output, I'm  not saying you must hit this number,  but at this rate, shouldn't your salary  be nearly doubling? Your salary needs  to double in five years, otherwise, you  won't be able to keep up with the  growth of per capita GDP. I’m not  talking about absolute totals, I’m  talking about the incremental growth;  this is exactly what’s happening with  many engineers in the Taiwanese market —their company compensation has  indeed nearly doubled compared to five  years ago. Of course, this creates  another problem in the market:  according to central bank statistics,  the average bank liquidity coverage  ratio has dropped to 122.9%this year,  the lowest since 2015. What does this  data mean? The concept is basically  whether the market's interbank  liquidity, especially highly liquid  assets, can cover potential capital  outflows over the next 30 days. The  legal minimum is 100. We still have  some time, but several banks are  getting close. For example, Land Bank  is at 102 and Sunny Bank is at 103,  while Mega Bank, SinoPac, Taiwan  Business Bank, and Shin Kong Bank have  already reached 107 to 109. So, funds  aren't exactly tight, but if you have  to say they are, it’s approaching a  liquidity risk. Banks naturally require  a certain safety ratio; you can't lend  out all your money, especially to  high-risk companies. Once capital  becomes tight, the pressure builds up.  Looking at it from this perspective,  money is flowing out and being lent out  a bit too quickly. That’s why the FSC  and regulators want banks to be more  cautious in selecting who they lend to,  rather than lending everything out. Now , circling back, didn't you say there  was an excess of idle capital? Excess  savings are at a record high; there’s  so much money and so many export orders , so how can banks be short on cash?  It's not that banks are out of money;  bank profits are actually hitting  record highs. It’s just that when you  compare the banks 'capital to market  demand, demand seems to be outpacing  the current rate of inflows, which is a  very interesting phenomenon. Money is  coming in very fast, but because banks  are screening their clients, they  prioritize lending to these companies,  which makes the pressure on individual  consumer credit feel much higher— it’s practically impossible to borrow . This is an interesting trend because  businesses have borrowed the money away . If we look at the details, in the  first seven months of this year, new  loans from Taiwanese banks have reached  4 trillion NTD, or about 126 billion  USD. July alone saw an increase of  nearly 1 trillion, and August and  September are showing even steeper  growth. If we break it down, about  115.2 billion of that consists of  syndicated loans. Many banks are  hesitant to lend to companies like TSMC  or MediaTek alone, so they partner up —Mega Bank, SinoPac, Land Bank, and  other public or commercial banks join  together to lend as a group; that's  what we call a syndicated loan. Then  there are convertible bonds, which are  linked to rising stock prices, and  another approach is raising capital  externally via GDRs, but the numbers  clearly show this capital is being used  for working capital. If we observe the  overall demand for working capital  between businesses and individuals, the  demand from businesses is roughly three  to four times that of the general  public. In other words, the scale of  corporate borrowing is nearly four  times that of personal credit or  collateral loans. Consequently, a vast  amount of money is borrowed by these  enterprises, leading to a "money crunch ." So, is there a money crunch for  businesses? Most companies are actually  securing funds; they aren't facing one,  but individuals are. Is there an  abundance of liquidity? Liquidity is  actually quite abundant, but market  demand is even stronger, which is what  causes this phenomenon called " liquidity surplus." That is correct,  because money keeps flowing in. However , this liquidity surplus is reflected  in asset prices. Once we feel that, we  think it’s difficult for us to borrow  money—it’s not exactly that  borrowing is difficult, but rather that  the money has already been taken by  these top-tier companies, who secure  better loan terms. As for us, we always  feel that the interest rates are  particularly high, and the total amount  of loans doesn't seem as large as we  imagined. Well, this is the actual  phenomenon we observe: while there is a  "money crunch" for individuals, the " liquidity surplus" refers to the  overall market. Looking at the Central  Bank’s statistics, the weighted  average interest rate for domestic bank  loans is now about 2.5%, a 17-year high .
